en: From time to time, one should recollect the Buddha.
The Preface to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "There are no two paths for returning to the source; there are many gates of expedient means.

It was solely through the diligent cultivation over vast eons by our World-Honored One that the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates for delivering sentient beings were perfectly accomplished, in order to guide and lead all beings within the Dharma-realm."

All are unified within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). As for the Three Pitakas and Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras left behind, what can be done with them while remaining in this world?
In the age of the Final Dharma, when the time since the Sage has long passed, how many ordinary people of meager merit can behold them? There are only licentious lyrics and minor songs.
They can enter through the ears and eyes; their deviant minds blaze intensely, and they remain unaware and unconscious as they create the three miserable realms.

Alas! Sentient beings wander through the river of craving and drift or sink within the ocean of karma. In the cycle of birth and death, they appear and vanish in an instant; yet they do not hear the Buddha-dharma.

When will there be an end to this? A single moment of heedlessness makes it difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas. (I) am personally ashamed of my heavy karma and deep obstructions, as well as my meager talent and shallow wisdom.

Being unversed in Confucian classics or phonology, I have instead used my worldly afflictions and distress as the impetus to compile this record of the joyful realms of the West according to the auspicious times of each month.
It is intended to serve as a self-restraint and exhortation for the practice of *nianfo*, so that beginners may enter the gate directly.
Every path is nothing other than the Moon’s pointing toward the way home; at all times, he reminds us of our original self.

I only wish that good men and faithful women may allow this to enter their storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) so that it may forever serve as the seed for the Way. If you are able to practice with faith, I pray that you will together be reborn in the Pure Land of the West.
Recorded by the Hermit of Yuchi on West Creek in Ancient Hangzhou, in the seventh month of the third year of the Guangxu era.
A Catalogue of Occasional Recitations of the Buddha’s Name;
Twelve Monthly Verses for Reciting the Buddha’s Name; Verses for Reciting the Buddha’s Name During the Twelve Periods of the Day.
Verses on Abstaining from Killing and Releasing Captured Creatures; Verses on Contentment and Following One’s Vocation;
A Diagram of the Jeweled Stupa for Cultivating the Mind and Rebirth; A Diagram of the Jeweled Stupa for Cultivating the Body and Attaining Buddhahood;
The Dream-Transmitted Exhortation to Women of the World to Recite the Buddha’s Name: An Account of Actual Realizations.
The Precious Verses on Purifying Oral Karma for Exhorting the World Transmitted in a Dream by Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
A Brief Account of Subduing Māra; The Inconceivable Merit of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
Verses on Abstinence from Sexual Misconduct; and Verses on the Original Nature.
Verses on Self-Remorse; Verses on Gathering the Mind for Mastery;
Verses on Visiting Mountains at Dawn; Verses on the Lazy Monk Reciting the Buddha’s Name;
Verses for Awakening the World; The Twelve Great Vows.
The supplementary verses state:
The *Jielashifangsheng luyao yan* (Essential Words on Refraining from Killing and Releasing Living Beings), The *Xiuxin rennai ke liuchuan* (Cultivating the Mind through Patience for Circulation),
And the *Xiaozigujie deng bianji* (Compilation of the Ancient Traces of Filial Sons) and others— These have never been included within this [present] collection.
At all times, those who study the pure karma of mindfulness of the Buddha should surely adorn their virtue; thus I describe our Buddha,
the Great Physician King of Compassion, who reveals the Pure Land and points toward the West.
Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma in person, With Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara attending at his sides;
The Buddhas of the six directions praise him with one voice, And the twelve hundred arhats rejoice beyond measure.
If a person’s mind remains undisturbed for even a single thought-moment, They shall surely be taught to ascend to the Lotus Land within seven days.
The sacred realms of the West are wondrous and inexhaustible; The Palace of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with the seven jewels.
Everywhere, gardens and groves are like brocade; Layer upon layer, pavilions and towers are as clear as jade.
Pairs of mandarin ducks proclaim sublime virtues; Couples of mynas chant the great names of the Dharma.
Amitābha has expounded the ultimate truth for me; In joy, I behold the sky-like face filled with smiles.
Desiring to enter the Western Land, my merit is no small thing; I shall take birth upon a lotus flower before the light of the world.
May all virtuous women transform their female forms; All who see or hear of this shall be named after the Dharma.
Adorned with the golden marks of the body, Holding hands, they roam together through the cities of the Buddha-lands.
All manner of joys and no hardships—this depends on the sincerity of one's vow.
If one has not yet returned to the Ultimate Bliss, one remains in Jambudvīpa; Drifting into the cycle of saṃsāra, suffering without end.
Even if you possess jade edicts and imperial decrees, Where can you seek them when your karmic rewards are exhausted?
It is better to cultivate the Pure Land while still alive; Do not let yourself lament before King Yama at the hour of death.
This Sahā world is no place for a soul to rest; Your true homeland lies only within the land of lotus blossoms.
The first month of the spring king marks the new year; everyone observes the full etiquette of the New Year’s greeting.
Children dress in the likeness of flower spirits, while beautiful women wear themselves like celestial nymphs.
Though the splendor before one's eyes is indeed fine, it is difficult to preserve the youthful countenance from aging.

The West is entirely the essence of longevity; It is not like the turbid heavens of Jambudvīpa, where the auspicious harmony of spring’s second month prevails. In the East, the rising sun warms and spreads its light;
All hundredfold activities and undertakings return to upright pursuits, As merchants transport their goods along the long river.
Green mountains and blue waters endure for a thousand years, Yet only this floating carcass is transient and short-lived.
I exhort all people of the world to turn back in time, To single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and reach the Lotus Land.
In the third lunar month, during Qingming, all things are in harmony; The peach blossoms and willow greens are a sight worth praising.
In this human realm, those with full blessings throughout their lives are few; In this world, those filled with grief and sorrow are many.
Seize the early opportunity to cultivate the Pure Land while alive; Do not let yourself regret your former choices after death.
The Buddha-dharma contains the method for peace and leisure; Do not listen to idle talk that undermines one's resolve.
In the fourth month, during the summer season, the weather is clear; Do not greedily crave flavors by slaughtering living beings.
Green grass half-buries those with rosy cheeks, While in the Yellow Springs many are seen who were black-haired in life.
It is all because of heavy karmic retribution for killing in past lives; The retribution for premature death in this life is manifest and clear.
When cleaning melons, fruits, bamboo shoots, and vegetables, they seem ten times more delicious than meat and pungent flavors.
When the fifth month arrives with the Dragon Boat Festival and the summer solstice, the world of red dust is truly pitiable;
the mother suffers hardship while the child is in her womb, like an iron Buddha sitting in a broken cart.
I urge you to seek the path of escape early; It is best to form a holy embryo within the Lotus Land.
In days to come, you shall personally travel to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Where you shall give birth to a jade infant amidst the flowers.
The June lotus reflects red upon the water; Princess Miaoshan has realized Perfect Penetration.
If the fire of ignorance does not arise within the mind, how could there be any warmth reaching the chest?
I urge you to recite the name of Amitābha early; when the mind is emptied through such recitation, the principle will naturally harmonize.
On that day, you shall personally attend the Lotus Pond assembly, where the true master will manifest within the flower.
At this time, encountering the most sorrowful month of the seventh, Maudgalyāyana went to the underworld to seek his mother;
with a single mind he sought to deliver his biological parent and established the Great Dharma Assembly of the Ullambana Bowl.
Though one may possess filial sons and virtuous grandsons, it all depends upon the strength of one’s own vow-power.
Only now do I realize the suffering of deluded thoughts and the cycle of rebirth; I vow that in this life I shall return to my native home.
On the Mid-Autumn Festival in the eighth month, the weather is cool; The wind blows through the vermilion cassias, carrying a faint fragrance.
Within the Sahā world, those who dwell in leisure are few; In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one’s lifespan is long.
I urge you to quickly make the vow for the Western Land, So as to avoid losing your composure at the moment of death.
Only then will you know the bitterness of being a traveler on the dusty road; Casting off your hands, you return westward to your native land.
On the Double Ninth of the ninth month, the chrysanthemums are yellow; When one encounters slander and defamation, it is most difficult to endure.
Loosen your belly and laugh "he-he"; let them speak foul words and act wildly.
Constantly and diligently sweep away delusive thoughts; do not forget Amitābha day by day.
When mindfulness reaches the emptiness of the mind, the Demon King retreats; Without even a snap of the fingers, one arrives in the Western Land.
In the cold skies of the tenth month, a northwest wind blows; Mengzong wept until he reached the bamboo grove.
These twenty-four acts of filial piety remain for all eternity, yet at the Lotus Pond, we do not meet as before.
Had you recited the name of Amitābha from the start, today mother and son would be together in compassionate countenance.
One child practices the Way and attains perfect enlightenment; The nine patriarchs are reborn together in the Pure Land.
At winter solstice, when the first yang-energy arises, the weather is cold; Sitting upright upon the meditation cushion, one dwells in stillness.
Moment by moment, Amitābha’s name fills the mind in silent tranquility; With every utterance of the Buddha’s name, delusions are extinguished.
Within, there is pure emptiness containing the moon of nature; Without, no worldly dust reaches the field of the mind.
If one recognizes this true pure land within, The numinous light shines through to the lotus in the Jade Pond.
Heavy snow falls thickly at the end of the twelfth month; Time passes like an arrow, swift as a shuttle.
As others bring parting gifts on the eve of the old year, do not concern yourself with the many greetings for the New Year;
instead, focus your mind with diligence on cultivating rebirth in the Pure Land. When the spiritual mechanism is fully penetrated and liberated, there is no need to seek it elsewhere.
Once the dust of delusion is swept away, Amitābha appears; you will soon arrive at the further shore of the Lotus Land.
At the third watch of the hour, one must be attentive to the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
Sitting quietly upon the meditation mat as dawn breaks, every sound of the Buddha’s name is a treasure for the body, Every phrase of Amitābha is the cause for transcending this world.
How can the Western Land be reached this very day? One should now pacify all delusive thoughts at once.
May I behold Amitābha face-to-face before returning to this Sahā world to deliver sentient beings;
do not let the recitation of the Buddha’s name slip away at dawn, nor waste your time in vain.
When the root-dusts are swept away, the flower of the mind will manifest; let no mundane sentiments arise and cast away all delusive thoughts.
Everywhere there is nothing that does not manifest one's own nature; In every instance, all is a river for crossing over others.
When you reach the day of passing the imperial examination with an empty mind, Entering the sacred and transcending the mundane occurs in a single kṣaṇa.
During the hours of the morning, apply yourself diligently to the recitation of the Buddha's name; A single phrase of Amitābha will then blend harmoniously beyond measure.
All phenomena are empty, and the Buddha-mind appears; Untainted by a single speck of dust, the six sense faculties are unimpeded.
If, through practice, one attains such a state, Why worry that the Pure Land will not be encountered?
Do not forget the vows of compassionate heart from the Dharma-treasury; He will surely come to welcome me back to my home.
At the hour of the snake, do not slacken your mindfulness of the Buddha; keep the four characters of the Great Name firmly in mind.
When going out, speak only of thoughts of home; when guests arrive, discuss only the old family traditions.
The Compassionate Mother of the Nine Lotuses gazes afar; this grieving son is utterly solitary on the dusty road.
In a single morning, having realized the truth, I am freed from this ephemeral body; mother and child meet, the joy profound.
At noon, my mindfulness of the Buddha only increases my heartache; suddenly tears fall to the edge of my lips.
In this Sahā world, a single bowl is difficult to sustain; in the Western Land, a hundred flavors appear before me.
I urge you to recite Amitābha’s name early, So as to avoid being dragged by karma amidst worldly toil.
There is no need to seek other mysterious or wondrous dharmas; Simply let this one thought be firm and steadfast.
When it is not yet time for the evening recitation and the sun slants toward the west, Sit quietly upon your meditation mat and think of your hometown.
I am ashamed of my own shallow learning and lack of monastic virtue; I envy the strength of the Way-power of those on neighboring mountains.
Were it not for the moon shining upon the clear, cold pond, How could the dust of defilement be wiped away and fully revealed?
I only wish that all fellow practitioners of goodness May enjoy constant auspiciousness throughout the six periods of day and night.
At the hour of Shen, the evening bell tolls as one recites the Buddha’s name; One must maintain mindfulness of impermanence at every thought.
This day has passed and life is diminished; I urge you to prepare for your future journey early.
Dedicate yourself with diligence to the recitation of Amitābha Buddha; Do not let worldly affairs weigh upon your mind.
Four characters are stored within the breast: The one hundred and eight bright pearls are the family treasure.
At the hour of You (the West), when reciting the Buddha’s name as the sun sinks, One must know that this Sahā world is a fiery pit;
If cause and effect are not clearly understood, it is true darkness, For impermanence does not provide a lantern for the journey.
I urge you to recite the name of Amitābha early; do not speak of the beauty of youthful rouge and powder.
In the West, there is no distinction between male and female; when practicing wondrous goodness, one is most youthful.
At the hour of the Dog, one must remain firm in mind while reciting the Buddha’s name; when one thinks of the solitary spirits, they are truly pitiable.
The cold winds blow bitterly with no refuge; Chilling rains fall as incense smoke ceases.
First practice yoga to offer this supreme dedication, And through the merit of a thousand halls, form auspicious karmic bonds.
Once I have personally beheld Amitābha, May you all together be delivered to the lotuses of the Jade Pond.
At the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), recite the Buddha’s name in serene stillness; Rest for a brief moment to nourish the spirit.
Amitābha is not obstructed by walking, sitting, or reclining; Within each breath, it is well to keep His name in mind.
As sleep comes on and the eyes grow dim, all Buddhas appear; The news from the Lotus Land reaches through this sound.
Awakening, it is already past the third watch; Unconsciously, my heart feels ten times more pure.
At the hour of midnight, reciting the Buddha’s name, the mind is most clear; Rising and sitting, donning my robes, my faith and vow are deep.
If for a single breath the life does not return, who am I? As soon as the six sense organs stir, they are but false and empty names.
Encountering conditions without grasping is not an obstruction; meeting objects without attachment, the mind is naturally at peace.
I vow that in this life I shall return to the Pure Land, to behold my Compassionate Father within the Lotus Kingdom.
At the hour of the Ox, I shall strike the signal bell to announce the time, offering prayers for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-fold longevity.
I pray again that the faithful patrons may increase in merit and longevity; May the world be blessed with peace and happiness.
Dedicate your minds and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with diligence; Make a vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
In the future, you shall awaken to and enter the purpose of the Lotus Realm, Thereby escaping the suffering of this Sahā world.
An inch of time is an inch of gold; I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and practice cultivation early.
Even with a body of jade leaves and golden pearls, one cannot avoid the form of wrinkled skin and white hair.
If you possessed the roots of faith from past lives, your aspiration would be earnest; if you lack wisdom in this present life, you will not turn your mind [from delusion].
When the day of my great destiny and final passing arrives, I shall come back as empty as I went;
I came as a monk, yet my delusions were many. I urge others to recite the Buddha’s name with ceaseless aspiration;
those of good faith who see or hear this will rejoice in their hearts, while the wicked will stir up storms within their bellies.
Feigning deafness as he opens his mouth in laughter, let him disregard good counsel;
yet if, through the karmic conditions of past lives, he now consents to believe, we shall ascend together to the other shore to behold Amitābha.
A Verse for Awakening the World to Abstinence from Killing.
Whenever the cock crows at dawn, the butcher rouses his cruel intent; he binds its four legs and thrusts a sharp blade into its neck.
In extreme agony it cries out, its blood flowing like a great flood.
Alas, its grievance is hard to tell as, in an instant, it appears before King Yama.
The boiling water is inherently heartless; Skin and hair are divided by the rain. The belly is ripped open and the head briefly falls;
The entrails are pulled out and the heart gouged with force. The five viscera each scatter apart; Where can the three souls remain?
Waiting only for this deed to be done— I ask you: is it fair or not?
Craving flavors for the sake of one's belly, Whether it be fish or meat— This one delights in ribs, that one loves pork heads.
Among the myriad goods, there are a hundred guests; A thousand cuts and a thousand carvings to sustain this life.
In this cycle, I fear the turning back.
A human body is most difficult to obtain; having obtained it, one encounters the Central Kingdom.
Yet, failing to contemplate performing virtuous deeds, one’s body and speech instead create evil. Though one may possess clever stratagems, they cannot avoid being seized by Impermanence.
When the Lord of Yama questions you, what words can you offer in reply?
By chance, the descendants are filial; Their attire is white as snow. The children weep piteously, and the virtuous daughter-in-law wails aloud.
Though the coffin is large and tall, It is difficult to properly fill every space within.
No longer pitying the love of former years, They bury him in the desolate wilderness.
Whether poor or rich, none can avoid reaching this point; at that time, one will suffer in grief and terror—rely on the Buddha to seek deliverance.
I exhort all people of the world: you must awaken early to the truth that the three realms are like a burning house; quickly seek the way out!
A Song of Contentment: Virtue alone is one’s treasure; Physical ease is itself happiness. Be content and do not resent poverty;
When there is no rice, even gruel will suffice. Pass the three meals with whatever is available; Why must one hoard and accumulate?

One lifetime without cold or hunger; A thousand or ten thousand feet of wealth, as rich as a rival state— Yet at the end of life, one cannot close one's eyes. For those of pure emptiness and detachment, there is neither honor nor shame;
The affairs of the world should be viewed with indifference; In setting one’s resolve, it must be firm and sincere.
Be upright and selfless; the Buddhas will rejoice and the spirits will submit in reverence.
All who practice the Way must first learn patience. When dwelling alone, delight in Chan meditation;
when living among others, strive for harmony. With simple greens and coarse tea, never loathe such plainness.
The plum blossoms spray forth their fragrance; A single turn of bitter cold penetrates to the very bone.
Those of bitter fate may enjoy honor and splendor, Yet their lifespan may prove insufficient.

If those with fortune are willing to cherish it, they shall receive heavenly emoluments in the future. Sever attachment and eliminate afflictions; One must read the scriptures until they are thoroughly mastered.
Failing to practice virtue while in this world, one’s efforts are in vain and merely empty toil.
Time passes with great rapidity; this illusory body does not endure long. Amidst the dust of the mundane world, once the days of youth have passed, the hair quickly turns white.
When the three-inch breath is severed, one meets King Yama empty-handed.
I exhort you to turn back now, To recite the name of Amitābha early on.
Practicing compassion and skillful means, Pass your years according to conditions. With a rectified mind, study the Buddha-way;
In your deeds, be neither vain nor frivolous. If you have wealth, it is fitting to provide relief; If you have no money, do not seek it by force.
When the fruits of goodness ripen in a single day, one leaps out from this suffering Saha world.
Verses on Cultivating the Body to Attain Buddhahood;
Verses on Cultivating the Mind for Rebirth.
This verse was personally transmitted by the golden mouth of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva within a dream.
Upon awakening, he washed his hands and, at a table, used inkstone, vermilion brush, and incense;
kneeling, he wrote it down, and thus this verse was completed. [He] wrote:
It was finished. As dawn approached in the east, the fragrance filled the room and his body and mind were refreshed and cool.
He prostrated toward the sky forty-eight times.
This occurred on the tenth day of the third month in the third year of the Guangxu era.

(Xu, surnamed Yang, of the Great Qing Dynasty; her Dharma name was Peifang. A native of Qiantang, she was compassionate, filial, patient, and gentle. Widowed at twenty-nine, she maintained her vow of chastity and took refuge in the Buddha. She cultivated the Pure Land practices with diligence, prostrating before the Five Classics and reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* morning and evening without interruption.

Daily she chanted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*. Later, because her elder brother invited her to reside in Jiangxi, she enjoyed the necessities of life there. Day and night she recited the Buddha’s name. One day, as she chanted through the middle of the night, she knelt upon her meditation mat and dozed off. In a state between waking and sleep, she beheld the two [Bodhisattvas] Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. )

The Great Being said, "Excellent, excellent! Your courageous diligence is entirely due to the roots of goodness cultivated in past lives. It is a pity that your allotted lifespan is not long; I shall grant you longevity, which shall extend further as you continue your practice.

However, because many people in this world do not understand cause and effect, those who cultivate goodness are few. I have a verse to exhort women; it is vital that you urge the women of the world to recite the Buddha’s name. When their merit is fulfilled and the fruit is perfected, I will come to receive them and lead them to see Amitābha.

Fearing that you might forget these instructions, I take ambrosia from the flask in my hand and place it in your mouth. In an instant, your body and mind become cool and refreshing. She prostrated herself before the Great Being a hundred times and, while reciting the verse, she regained consciousness.

In brief, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is no trivial matter. When internal and external māras disturb the True Dharma, one lacks a sovereign master and becomes attached to objects of craving; moved by these objects, one falls into the net of Māra.
What was originally a virtuous cause turns instead into misfortune; those who study the Way must be cautious and on guard.
The fool has opened up four points regarding the meaning of discerning demons: one must examine oneself and investigate with great care.
First, karmic obstacles caused by past grudges manifest as demons.
Throughout distant kalpas and even in this present life within the ranks of ordinary beings, I have failed to practice loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, righteousness, and propriety;
instead, through killing, stealing, lust, falsehood, greed, anger, and delusion, I have bound myself with many enemies whom I encounter today.
If you study the Great Way and come to disturb me, it will be able to obstruct the Holy Path so that success is not achieved.
Unable to bear such long-standing enmity, I entreat the Triple Gem and pay homage to the Golden Countenance;
with shame and sincerity, I pray for repentance. The enemy shall naturally retreat and vanish without a trace.
I then resolve upon four great vows to universally benefit all sentient beings within the Pure Land.
The second external affliction is caused by demonic persons who create obstacles;
petty people without cause fabricate idle slander, causing practitioners of the Way to live in unease.
These demons do not come to disturb them for any other reason; it is entirely because [the practitioner] lacks propriety or possesses insufficient influence.
Whether it be arrogance or blunt speech, coarse conduct, or relying on power with a narrow mind;
if one praises oneself while speaking of others' faults, or lacks patience and a gentle countenance,
one will consequently invite harsh words and much slander, which disrupts the cultivation of the mind and obstructs the original source.
Those who aspire to the Way should avoid [worldly distractions] below; Withdraw from oneself to nurture virtue, remaining patient and at peace.
(Verse 3) The Mara of verbal karma acts as a mad obstruction;
This Mara of verbal karma creates madness and obstructions, Causing one to be unfrugal with speech and to follow after external traces.
Excessive talk saps one's spirit and exhausts the spleen; A scattered mind prevents the true nature from manifesting.
To discuss the abstruse and the wondrous, or lecture on religion and doctrine, Is to boast of one’s own enlightenment while regarding others as ignorant and deluded.
To compose poems and lyrics at whim, Is to turn from being fierce and evil in the past to being virtuous and wise in the present.

To discuss the long and short of others, to speak of right and wrong, To impartially debate the rise and fall of states and dynasties from ancient times to the present—these do not concern one's own affairs, yet they provoke empty anger. To slander behind one’s back while praising to one’s face is mere opportunism;
All such evil speech causes the loss of right mindfulness. Those who practice the Way must strictly avoid them.
Not only does frugality in speech nurture virtue, but it also prevents the mind from becoming agitated and disturbed.
Regarding the fourth affliction, the demon of the suffering of illness creates obstacles through suffering;
this demon of illness causes many physical ailments due to karmic transgressions.
If one loses self-regulation, a hundred ailments may arise; the fool enumerates several rules for preemptive self-protection:
Regulate the spleen and stomach by selecting food and drink; Be sparing of rich flavors and avoid raw or cold foods.
Do not sleep immediately after eating, eat little at night, Do not carry heavy loads when full, and do not recite scriptures on an empty stomach.
Eat little of the five flavors; avoid improper substances. Do not crave fried or roasted foods; avoid those that are rotten, putrid, or damp.
Practice *zazen* (seated meditation) in a humid place; sleep in a breezy spot. After sweating, do not enter water; after exposure to heat, do not seek immediate coolness.
Do not bathe while facing the wind; do not lie down under the stars. Avoid extreme hunger, extreme satiety, and excessive joy or anger.
Extreme cold, extreme heat, heavy rain, and dew— When internal injuries and external infections are both neglected, Various sores and ailments arise, leaving the body in unrest.
I universally exhort you: you must take precautions in advance.
The above four points briefly enumerate the māras; To examine their details, consult the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
How many practitioners in this world Are hindered by the suffering of illness from the true source!
They all say there are no prohibitions regarding food and drink, Yet they have been driven to utter confusion for years.
Twenty years ago, before this, I refused to listen to or believe the words of the ancients.
Following one's whims and desires without restraint, One most delights in sourness and stench, craving putridity and decay.
For many years plagued by numerous ailments, Like a shattered vessel or broken bowl, seeking physicians and taking medicine to no avail; All labor is wasted, all wealth squandered.
Up to now, through testing and verification, the principles have been understood; the illness has completely healed and the body is at peace.
If anyone can rely upon this verse, it will protect them so that all calamities are entirely eliminated.
The merit of reciting the Buddha’s name is inconceivable.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means; To recite and prostrate without artifice is difficult to describe.
Though one may not commit evil deeds during life, At the moment of death, all is pitch-black darkness.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means; In the Tang Dynasty, there was a Bai Juyi.
Five people, husband and wife alike, have practiced the Way together; To this day they remain within the lotus of the Jade Pond.
The single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" is the most expedient means; It requires no labor and costs no money.
Provided one practices it throughout one's entire life without interruption, Why worry about not reaching the presence of the Dharma King?
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means; Do not say that household affairs have never been neglected.
With hands busy with one’s livelihood and mouth reciting the Buddha’s name, At the end of life, one departs for the Western Heaven carrying one’s karma.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means; Yet the enmities of many lifetimes manifest before one.
Shao Biao dreamed that amidst extreme terror he chanted aloud: "Oyster shells transform into sparrows to be reborn in heaven;
The single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means. Whether bird or beast, human or deva, Even a starling can understand and join the mouth of a monk in recitation;
Buried in level ground after death, it emerges as a blue lotus."
The single phrase "Amitābha" is the most expedient means; Ten recitations can transcend the barrier of birth and death.
Only those who lack faith and slander the Dharma are excluded; All others who possess the vow will surely be born in the lotus.
The single phrase "Amitābha" is the most expedient means; Even small children can easily speak it.
Though one may have a mouth but no mind for recitation, there is a karmic affinity upon the Lotus Pond;
a single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient means.
Whether in red or black, in light or dark rooms, as long as one’s sincere faith and vow are earnest, at that moment hell will transform into a lotus.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the most expedient; Those who do not believe are truly pitiable.
They辜负 (gu fù) the compassionate vow of our Buddha, And at the moment of death, they still fall into the Avīci Hell.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the most direct and swift; In the past, Sudhana visited spiritual teachers.
He went to visit the youth De-yun, who showed him that reciting the Buddha’s name brings about samādhi;
this single phrase concerning Amitābha is the most direct and expedient path. In the Song dynasty there was a man named Wu Tzu-ts'ai who said:
"There is no peace within the three realms; one cannot remain there. The Western Pure Land has lotus wombs."
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most direct and swift path;
Regardless of the ten evils or even the five heinous crimes, When Guang'e first turned his mind back toward the Way, He set down his butcher’s blade and later attained Buddhahood.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most direct and swift path; Past evil karma can be easily extinguished thereby.
The couple Liu Guang turned their hearts back to the Way; In six years, their merit was perfected and they attained Buddhahood together.
A single phrase of Amitābha is most capable of transcending [suffering]; Even the karma of killing can be easily eliminated.
Before Shanhe had even finished ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, The herd of oxen retreated and perished, leaving him at ease.
A single phrase of Amitābha is most capable of transcending; The various discursive thoughts within the breast can easily be eliminated.
In the Song dynasty there was a Huang the Blacksmith; To this day he enjoys carefree ease in the Pure Land.
A single phrase of Amitābha is most capable of transcending; The path across ten million billion lands is not far.
Six times a day, prostrations and mindfulness continue without interruption; A single phrase of Amitābha is the most accessible path to transcendence.
Wu, Qiong, Nie, and Ju all attained rebirth—this is not the idle talk of one who is lazy or dull-witted;
Their names are inscribed upon the *Biographies of Those Reborn in the Pure Land*.
Do not be indolent regarding the single phrase of Amitābha; Keep it constantly present in your mind until the end of life without interruption.
If you do not reach the Pure Land at the moment of death, Take refuge early in the single phrase of Amitābha; In your practice, you must learn the rites of the Śākya family.
Reverently bowing and mindful in accordance with the Dharma, One will certainly not remain within the three realms.
Do not be indolent regarding even a single phrase of Amitābha; Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, may one always be at ease.
May I quickly attain the lowest of the low grades, And pray that I shall never be born outside of the Western Land.
A Verse on Abstinence from Sexual Misconduct: The flower streets and willow alleys are most pitiable; Only the mind’s greedy attachments are difficult to describe.
Powdered rouge adorns faces in a thousand ways; Dragon-flower and musk perfume garments with a hundred charms.
Three inches of breath remain amidst much joy and love; Once impermanence strikes, it is unbearable to behold.
I urge you to seek early the plan for purity and peace; Do not envy the half-life of an immortal in the red dust.
A Verse on One's Original Nature.
The physical marks of women in this world are natural; Within the mouth, the names they call out are of two kinds.
If one practices without knowing what lies beyond the body, How could there be leisure to contemplate women and men?
The Great Way originally has no form or appearance; One should view all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm as one body.
The true source is profound stillness, yet the void is shattered; man and ox leave no tracks, and the moon is solitary and full.
I am ashamed of myself for dwelling in a quiet mountain hermitage; throughout my life, I have never sought the攀缘 (pān-yuán) of sensory attachments.
At times I am constantly short of firewood and rice; I have no guests coming and going, nor do I have any money.
Some praise me while others slander me; some show me respect while others loathe me.
There is but one phrase, Amitābha Buddha, which I reverently recite day and night, never daring to be idle.
To gather the mind, mastery requires freedom from obstruction; to master it, one must be free from sorrow. To abide in one's fundamental nature, wherever one stays is leisurely;

those who shave their heads and become disciples should stay but briefly, for afflictions are few. If one takes refuge [in worldly things], attachments increase; if one pursues right and wrong, complications multiply.
Circumstances and dharmas are inevitably manifold, and the mind is bound to be distracted; Profit and fame are difficult to sever, and the Path is hard to cultivate.
When seeking others, it is better to seek oneself; Rather than dwelling on worldly sentiments, one should contemplate Amitābha and pay homage at sacred mountains in the morning.
Ascending the mountain and crossing the sea requires a firm resolve; Go wherever you may, following conditions as they arise.
Everywhere there are riverside streams and wild greens that can never be exhausted; Along the road, withered firewood can never be fully consumed.
In the breast, there is only the single phrase "Buddha"; Within the waist-bag, it has been washed clean until not a half-copper coin remains.
When weary, I sleep in my robes beneath a tree; Upon waking, the bright moon shines upon my breast.
The slothful monk’s verse:
the slothful monk’s poverty and suffering are beyond words; Yellow radish soup and plain rice are not always provided in full measure.
In my hands I still hold the hundred-and-eight beads; Upon my body remains but half a garment.
In my heart I keep the name of the Buddha in mind; Beyond this, there is no further entanglement or distraction.
If anyone asks me how much merit I have achieved, Even the single phrase "Namo Amitābha" is not yet complete.
A Verse for Awakening the World:
At all times, one must first take mindfulness of the Buddha as essential. This ephemeral, illusory body is not firm or enduring;
In the mountains, one often sees trees a thousand years old, Yet in this world, it is rare to live even a hundred years.
How many who were clever are buried in the green grass; how many who were foolish have gone to the Yellow Springs.
Whether praying for sons, praying for daughters, or praying for longevity—why not instead pray for the Pure Land?
The Twelve Great Vows.

Reaching out with my hand, I pluck forth a single incense pellet; Without substance, without fire, and without smoke, The source of this fragrance arises from the Pure Land, Its sprout is lodged in the bottomless sky of Sahā.
Burned within the incense burner as an offering to the Buddha, It reaches the assembly of Bodhisattvas at the Lotus Pond.
I pray that the Compassionate Honored One will come to protect and aid me, fulfilling my compassionate vows swiftly and completely.
May the Emperor live for ten thousand years; may the foundation of his merit and the Dragon Throne be perpetually transmitted.
May the Empress and the Crown Prince both reach a thousand years; may the golden branches and jade leaves rejoice in their perfect harmony.
Second, may the wishes of the sovereign and his high ministers be fulfilled, with virtuous generals and loyal subjects transmitted through the generations to protect the imperial carriage,
the state, and the Buddha-dharma, increasing merit, longevity, and boundless joy. Third,
may the provinces, capitals, prefectures, and counties be unified under governance, protecting the nation and pacifying the people, transmitted from generation to generation.
May the civil and military officials increase in rank and emolument; may the noble relatives of each office enjoy long lives.
Fourthly, may the three calamities be extinguished throughout the world, and may the Three Teachings flourish to produce sages and worthies.
May the winds and rains be harmonious and the people live in peace and joy; may there be eternal celebration of great abundance in every place.
May the five vows each dwell in hermitages, pavilions, and monasteries; may the mountain gates be pure and the Dharma boundless.
May those who shave their heads and receive ordination successively transmit the Triple Gem; may the Sangha attain the fruit of Buddhahood and the Way lead to the state of the Immortal.
May the six vows inspire the faithful assembly of men and women, who take refuge in the Triple Gem with firm resolve in the Way.
May those who seek and those who respond swiftly attain Buddhahood; May there be no demons or obstacles, and may you be born early upon the lotus.
May every person possess the Buddha-nature; May there be no misfortune or evil, and may the virtuous mind remain firm.
May there be no poverty, no suffering, and no untimely death; May there be wealth and children, and may blessings flow on endlessly.
Eighth, I pray that all men throughout the world shall know cause and recognize effect, making filial piety their priority;
may there be no widowers and no bachelors, and no calamities or hardships; may they always possess both boats and oars in full measure.
Ninth, I pray that the women of the world shall be virtuous, gentle, and mild, with countenances like those of immortals.
May there be no orphans, no widows, and no untimely deaths; May roots, leaves, fruits, and flowers all flourish.

Through these ten vows, may the dead—whether male or female—be delivered; May those in the six realms and four modes of birth all ascend to heaven, And may the hells be transformed into realms of carefree ease, While the Blood Lake is transmuted into a jeweled lotus pond.
Eleventh: May my lifespan be complete, and may the supreme realm of the West appear before me;
seven days prior, may I know it myself, change my robes, and through mindfulness of the Buddha, return to heaven.
Twelfth: May I, at the moment of death, be received by the assembly of sages to the lotus flower of the Jade Pond.
But as soon as I beheld Amitābha, I returned to this Sahā world to launch the Dharma-ship.
Having completed my prayers for indolent monks, I pray that the merit and longevity of all may be perfected.
May I swiftly fulfill my vow for Bodhi, and together with others ascend to the Western Heaven, reaching the other shore.
May these merits be universally extended to all; may we and those who share our faith together attain the Way of Buddhahood.
